title: Lamb Tagine
subtitle: Slow-cooked Moroccan lamb with warming spices
excerpt: A good lamb tagine is one of the most rewarding slow cooks in the repertoire: lamb shoulder braised until falling apart in a deeply spiced sauce fragrant with cinnamon, cumin, and saffron. It needs time rather than attention, making it ideal for feeding a crowd. Dried apricots are a traditional addition; the note in the method explains how to incorporate them.
sourceNotes: The tagine is both a cooking vessel and a category of dish central to Moroccan cuisine. Slow-cooked meat with aromatic spices, preserved lemon, and dried fruit has been a cornerstone of North African cooking for centuries, with regional variations found across Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: This tagine tastes even better the next day. Make it a day ahead and reheat gently.
recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months.

content.text: Brown the lamb in batches before adding anything else. That caramelised crust is where the depth of flavour comes from. Dried apricots are traditional: stir in 100 g about 30 minutes before the end for a sweet note. Use a large casserole or heavy saucepan, not a clay tagine.

items.prepNote: steeped in 2 tbsp of warm water

content.text: Steep the saffron in 2 tablespoons of warm water and set aside. Pat the lamb chunks dry with kitchen paper and season well with salt and pepper.

Heat a large, heavy-bottomed saucepan or casserole over high heat with a drizzle of oil. Brown the lamb in batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side, until deeply caramelised on all surfaces. Do not crowd the pan. Remove and set aside.

Reduce the heat to medium and add the sliced onions to the same pan. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until softened and lightly golden. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for a further 2 minutes.

Add the ground cinnamon, cumin, coriander, and turmeric. Stir for 1 minute until the spices are fragrant and coating the onions. Pour in the tinned tomatoes, chicken stock, saffron water, and honey. Stir well and add the lemon zest.

Return the browned lamb to the pan. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to low. Cover tightly and cook for 1 hour 45 minutes to 2 hours, stirring every 30 minutes, until the lamb is very tender and the sauce has thickened.
If adding dried apricots, stir them in about 30 minutes before the end of cooking. In the last 10 minutes, remove the lid to allow the sauce to reduce and thicken slightly if needed.
Taste and adjust seasoning. Add the lemon juice to brighten the sauce. Scatter over fresh coriander and serve with couscous, flatbreads, or rice.

items.symptom: The lamb is tough after 2 hours of cooking
items.cause: The heat was too high, causing the muscle fibres to seize rather than break down slowly. Lamb shoulder needs low, gentle heat to become tender.
items.fix: Turn the heat down to its lowest setting and cook for a further 30 minutes. The lamb should eventually relax and become tender. A fully covered pan is important: if the lid does not fit tightly, cover with foil underneath it.

items.symptom: The sauce is watery and thin
items.cause: The liquid has not had enough time to reduce, or the lid was left on throughout without giving the sauce a chance to thicken.
items.fix: Remove the lid for the last 15 to 20 minutes of cooking to allow evaporation. If still thin after that, remove the lamb with a slotted spoon and boil the sauce over medium heat for 5 to 10 minutes until it coats the back of a spoon.

items.symptom: The tagine tastes flat and lacks depth
items.cause: The lamb was not browned properly at the start, which is where most of the savoury depth in this dish comes from.
items.fix: For future batches, dry the meat thoroughly and brown it in very small batches over high heat. A crowded pan steams rather than sears. Adding a teaspoon of tomato paste with the spices also helps build depth.
